clue.text: Blast, the Beachy Head beacon !

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so take the opening letter of Beachy

parts.note: a beacon is a signal light

explanation.surface: An exclamation about the lighthouse warning light on the chalk cliffs of Beachy Head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beachy Head' looks like the place name, but 'Head' asks for the first letter of 'Beachy', B. Beachy Head is a headland on the south coast of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A blast and a blight are both a withering disease or a ruinous influence on crops and hopes.

clue.text: It looked deadly,

parts.note: a creature of legend whose mere gaze was said to kill

explanation.surface: Something appeared dangerous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'looked deadly' reads as 'seemed dangerous', but the legendary serpent's look itself was deadly.
explanation.definitionFit: A mythical serpent-king whose stare killed anyone it met.

clue.text: Maroon' one sun goddess

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
Sol is Latin for the sun and the Roman sun god
Ate is the Greek goddess of folly and ruin

explanation.surface: A lone sun goddess is stranded somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maroon' looks like the colour, but it is the verb, to strand someone; 'sun goddess' is not one piece but two, SOL and ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To maroon someone is to leave them cut off on a desert island, alone and apart.

clue.text: But not the upper-class Scots' sole preserve

definitions.text: But not the upper-class Scots' sole preserve

parts.words: But not the upper-class Scots' sole preserve
parts.note: the 'high' Scots suggests the gentry, but the mountain country belongs to every Scot

explanation.surface: A protest that something is not reserved only for the Scottish gentry.
explanation.walkthrough: The mountainous north of Scotland sounds like it should belong to 'high' Scots, the upper class, but it does not.
explanation.definitionFit: The mountainous north and west of Scotland, home to Scots of every class.

clue.text: Hot day for a speed fiend

explanation.surface: A sweltering day is described as just the thing for someone who loves driving fast.
explanation.definitionFit: A very hot day is informally a scorcher, and a reckless fast driver or cyclist was also called a scorcher.

clue.text: Righting' wrongs ? Sound idea!

parts.note: said aloud, 'righting wrongs' could be 'writing wrongs', mistakes made by office clerks

explanation.surface: A suggestion that putting injustices right is a sensible plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Righting wrongs' sounds the same as 'writing wrongs', which are mistakes of the pen.
explanation.definitionFit: Slips made in copying or record-keeping by office workers.

clue.text: Dispatch takes time to come up right on 'top

indicators.note: in a down clue, on top places one piece above the other
in a down entry, coming up means the word time is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Sending something off takes a while before the right result surfaces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to come up' turns TIME into EMIT, and 'on top' places R above it.
explanation.definitionFit: To remit is to send off, as money is sent to a creditor.

clue.text: The lady's case, we hear, applies' to Esau

definitions.note: a description standing for an adjective

indicators.note: we hear signals that the phrase is to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: her suit, a woman's lawsuit or case in court

explanation.surface: A woman's legal case is reported to concern Esau.
explanation.walkthrough: Esau in Genesis was 'a hairy man', so the adjective applies to him.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible Esau was born covered in hair, so hairy describes him.

clue.text: Depended on getting a priest into debt

indicators.note: into says one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: being in the red means being in debt
Eli was the priest at Shiloh who raised Samuel

explanation.surface: Someone relied on a priest to get them into debt.
explanation.walkthrough: RED stands for debt because overdrawn accounts were printed in red ink.
explanation.definitionFit: Relying on someone means trusting or counting on them.

clue.text: Father to be or not to be?. Ask the daughter

parts.note: pop is an informal word for father

parts.words: to be or not to be?
parts.note: Hamlet's soliloquy goes on 'that is the question'

explanation.surface: A father agonises over his existence, then consults his daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: To ask for a daughter's hand is to propose marriage; Hamlet's line 'To be or not to be: that is the question' supplies the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Proposing marriage, traditionally asking a young woman to become one's wife.

clue.text: Wavy bird goes West soon perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be arranged some other way, an anagram signal

explanation.surface: A bird with rippling plumage is heading west before long, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wavy' looks like a description of the bird's flight, but 'wavey' is a North American name for this goose, so 'Wavy bird' is the whole definition and 'perhaps' rearranges GOES + W + SOON.
explanation.definitionFit: Canadian hunters call this white Arctic goose a 'wavey', from its Cree name.

clue.text: No hanging for this picture

parts.note: a picture painted straight onto a wall never needs a hook or a frame to hang from

explanation.surface: A gallery note says this particular picture is not to be hung.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No hanging' reads like a ban on execution or a gallery rule, but the picture cannot be hung because it is painted on the wall itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A wall painting is part of the plaster, so it is never hung like a framed canvas.

clue.text: Minor publication coming out in Spring ?

explanation.surface: A small pamphlet is due to be issued in the spring season.
explanation.definitionFit: A printed handout is a small folded sheet, and a young unfolding leaf also bears the name, appearing in springtime.

clue.text: To gate-crash in the beginning-—unmannerly

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, here of the word the

parts.note: unmannerly means rude, lacking good manners

explanation.surface: Barging uninvited into a party right from the start is ill-mannered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the beginning' gives T, the first letter of 'the', and sits between IN and RUDE.
explanation.definitionFit: To gate-crash is to force your way in where you are not invited, to barge in.

clue.text: Some yarn of birds like the 10 in flight ?

explanation.surface: A tale about geese in flight, like the snow goose at 10.
explanation.definitionFit: A coil of wool is called a skein, and so is a flock of wild geese flying in formation.

clue.text: Once an underground worker, making us try our level best ?

definitions.text: making us try our level best
definitions.note: a phrase describing a person who sets tests, standing for a noun

parts.note: ex means former, what something once was
a miner works below ground in a pit

explanation.surface: A former coal miner has become someone who tests us to our limits.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: the one who makes candidates try their level best is the person setting and marking the exam.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sets and marks a test is the person whose paper forces candidates to do their utmost.

clue.text: Fashionable hair-style many violated

parts.note: in means fashionable
a fringe is hair cut straight across the forehead
D is the Roman numeral 500, a crossword shorthand for many

explanation.surface: A trendy haircut has been ruined by a crowd of people.
explanation.definitionFit: Infringed rules or rights have been breached or broken.

clue.text: Get rid of 'a badly set joint

indicators.note: badly set means arranged wrongly, so the letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A doctor discards a joint that has been set wrongly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly set joint' reads as a medical mishap, but 'badly' rearranges SET JOINT.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw something overboard or discard it as unwanted.

clue.text: Rubber from a ship in a French river

indicators.note: in tells us that one piece is placed inside the river's name

parts.note: the Meuse is a river rising in France and flowing through Belgium
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: Something rubbery salvaged from a vessel sunk in a French river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubber' suggests the material, but it is a person who gives massages.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who gives massages rubs her clients' muscles.

clue.text: Pretends facts about Smith are unusual

indicators.note: are unusual tells us the letters are put in an odd order

parts.note: F. E. Smith, Lord Birkenhead, was a famous lawyer and politician

explanation.surface: Someone says the facts about a man named Smith are strange.
explanation.walkthrough: F. E. Smith was a British lawyer and politician; 'about' joins FE to FACTS, and 'are unusual' rearranges the whole.
explanation.definitionFit: To affect a manner is to put it on or feign it.

clue.text: Somerset's corollary to Devon's Westward Ho !?

definitions.text: Somerset's corollary to Devon's Westward Ho !?

parts.words: Somerset's corollary to Devon's Westward Ho !?
parts.note: a Somerset town whose name read as two words says 'starting at the east', the natural partner to a cry of heading west

explanation.surface: Somerset is said to have its own counterpart to the Devon resort of Westward Ho!
explanation.walkthrough: Westward Ho! is a seaside village in Devon; the Somerset town's name splits as FROM E, 'from the east', which is where anyone going westward starts.
explanation.definitionFit: A market town in Somerset whose name splits into two words meaning out of the east.

clue.text: Mineral sources set up by a Greek playboy

parts.note: ores are rocks from which minerals or metals are extracted

indicators.note: up in a down entry means the word set is read upwards

explanation.surface: A Greek playboy has had mining rights set up for him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playboy' is read as play + boy: the young hero of Greek tragedies by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides.
explanation.definitionFit: Agamemnon's son, the central young man of several ancient Greek plays.

clue.text: "We are the —— men" (Eliot)

parts.note: the missing word from the first line of T. S. Eliot's 1925 poem

explanation.surface: A line from a T. S. Eliot poem with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan shows a dash where the answer belongs: the poem begins 'We are the hollow men / We are the stuffed men'.
explanation.definitionFit: T. S. Eliot's poem is titled The Hollow Men, from its opening line.

clue.text: Business premises usual with houses advertised

explanation.surface: Estate agents' adverts for commercial buildings follow a standard form.
explanation.walkthrough: Old house adverts promised 'the usual offices', meaning kitchen, scullery and lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: Commercial workplaces are rooms for clerical work, and in property listings the term meant the service rooms of a house.

clue.text: Beer-consuming Bath companion came to land of milk and honey

definitions.text: came to land of milk and honey
definitions.note: a description standing for a person's name

indicators.note: consuming means one piece takes the other inside it

parts.note: CB is Companion of the Order of the Bath, a British honour
ale is a type of beer

explanation.surface: A beer-drinking companion from Bath arrived in a land of plenty.
explanation.walkthrough: Caleb was one of the spies Moses sent into Canaan, the land 'flowing with milk and honey', and one of the two of his generation who entered it.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Numbers this spy reached Canaan and later settled there.

clue.text: In term, a change of clothing

indicators.note: a change of the letters means they are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: During the school term, someone needs a fresh set of clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a change of clothing' reads as a fresh outfit, but 'change of' rearranges the letters of IN TERM A.
explanation.definitionFit: An old literary word for garments or attire.

clue.text: Do licensed victuallers form this government?

definitions.text: Do licensed victuallers form this government?

parts.words: Do licensed victuallers form this government?
parts.note: council-level rule shares its name with the neighbourhood pub, and publicans run pubs

explanation.surface: A question whether publicans make up a certain tier of the state.
explanation.walkthrough: Licensed victuallers are British pub landlords; the nearby pub is your 'local', and the council is 'local government'.
explanation.definitionFit: Council-level administration is local government, and the neighbourhood pub is everyone's local.

clue.text: Makes desert blossom with 'strange rites round Latvian capital

indicators.note: round says the rearranged letters go around the capital
strange means the letters of the word rites are made odd, rearranged

parts.note: Riga is the capital of Latvia

explanation.surface: Someone coaxes the desert into flower with odd ceremonies around the Latvian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Latvian capital' looks like L, but it is the city RIGA, which goes inside IRTES, the anagram of RITES signalled by 'strange', wrapped by 'round'.
explanation.definitionFit: Watering dry land through channels lets crops grow where there was none, making arid ground bloom.

clue.text: Desire some. Burgundy, say, with a bit of chicken

parts.note: to desire is to wish

indicators.note: say signals that the wine's name is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: Beaune is a Burgundy wine, named after its town

explanation.surface: Someone longs for a glass of Burgundy to go with their chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: The Burgundy wine Beaune is said 'bone'; 'say' gives the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: The forked breastbone of a fowl, pulled apart for a wish.

clue.text: Boy, is getting on as an inventor

parts.note: Ed is a boy's name, short for Edward

explanation.surface: A young man is getting on in his career as an inventor.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse is a charade: ED, IS and ON in order, with 'getting' and 'as' as links.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Alva Edison invented the phonograph and a practical light bulb.
